source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Karl Popper (Thornton)
finding: Popper proposed falsifiability as the line between science and non-science. A theory that no possible observation could contradict is not scientific. Main targets were psychoanalysis and Marxism.
numbers: Logik der Forschung 1935; English 1959; Conjectures and Refutations 1963.
quote: if a theory is incompatible with possible empirical observations it is scientific
limits: Demarcation, not a theory of how scientists actually work. Critics say it is too strict and too loose.
agent_relevance: G3 and S4 rest on this: a check only counts if it could have failed.

source: SEP: Karl Popper (corroboration, content, severity)
finding: A theory is corroborated, never verified, and only when it survives a risky prediction that could have failed. Content and probability vary inversely: improbable, informative theories are more testable. This is the logic behind 'bold conjecture'.
numbers: No numeric measure in the text; Popper's corroboration is not a probability.
limits: The SEP page does not define 'bold conjectures' or give a formula for severity; those come from Popper's own books, not opened here.
agent_relevance: Prefer tests with a real chance of failure; a pass on an easy test adds little (matches G3).

source: SEP: Karl Popper (basic statements)
finding: Falsification needs singular, testable statements, but testing stops at statements we decide to accept. Popper compares this to a jury verdict that can be revised. So falsification is never fully mechanical.
numbers: Reference: Popper 2002 p.86.
quote: testing must stop at some basic statement or other which we decide to accept
limits: This is a convention, which critics treat as a hidden weak point.
agent_relevance: The agent's checker output is the 'accepted basic statement'. The checker must itself be trusted and revisable (G2).

source: SEP: Karl Popper (verisimilitude)
finding: Popper tried to rank false theories by closeness to truth. In 1974 David Miller and Pavel Tichy each showed the definition fails for any two false theories. Popper conceded the point in 1979.
numbers: Two independent refutations in 1974.
limits: No accepted replacement is settled in the page text.
agent_relevance: Do not build a numeric 'closeness to truth' score from falsification alone. Count failures and survivals instead.

source: SEP: Karl Popper (Duhem-Quine, ad hoc rescue, Lakatos)
finding: A failed prediction does not say which assumption is wrong (Putnam 1974). Lakatos: theories sit inside a protective belt of auxiliary hypotheses. Popper banned ad hoc rescues at first, later allowed some (Uranus motion).
numbers: Lakatos 1978; Putnam 1974.
limits: The Duhem-Quine name is not used in the page; the issue is covered under auxiliary hypotheses.
agent_relevance: When a test fails, locate the failing part from real output (G2) before dropping the whole answer; a rescue must make a new testable claim.

source: SEP: Scientific Method (Popper falsificationism section)
finding: Falsification is deductive; confirmation by instances commits affirming the consequent. Corroboration measures survived testing, not probability of truth. Later Popper accepted 'immunizations' and spoke of degrees of testability (1985).
numbers: Cites Popper 1959, 1963, 1985 p.41f.
limits: Page does not discuss severity, Duhem-Quine or strong inference in the part read.
agent_relevance: Supports the asymmetry: a failed check is stronger evidence than a passed one.

source: Mayo (2019) Statistical Inference as Severe Testing: abstracts and keywords
finding: Mayo's minimal severity rule: if little has been done to rule out flaws in taking data as evidence for a claim, the claim has not passed a severe test. She credits Popper's insight but says he fell short on corroboration, Duhem's problem and demarcation, and builds a post-Popper account on error probabilities.
numbers: Excursion 2 Tour II covers Popper, falsification, corroboration and Duhem's problem. Book abstract only, not the full text.
quote: If little has been done to rule out flaws in taking data as evidence for a claim, then that claim has not passed a severe test.
limits: Abstract-level reading only. Severity is defined in error-statistics terms, which Bayesians contest.
agent_relevance: Gives a usable test of a check: would it have probably failed if the answer were wrong? Fits G3.

source: Wason (1960) On the failure to eliminate hypotheses in a conceptual task (as summarised in Jhaveri et al. 2026)
finding: Founding 2-4-6 task. People saw 2-4-6, were told it fit a hidden rule, proposed triples and got yes/no. Most tested triples that fit their own guess (e.g. more even-by-2 sequences), became confident, and missed that the rule was just 'any increasing sequence'.
numbers: 29 participants: 6 announced the right rule first time, 21 eventually found it. Mean ratio of disconfirming to confirming tests: 1.79 for first-time-correct, 0.24 for first-wrong, 0.50 vs 0.19 on second try.
limits: Numbers are as re-reported by Jhaveri et al.; Wason's paper itself was not opened. Hidden rule is broader than the hypothesis, the one case where positive tests are uninformative.
agent_relevance: Basic failure to guard against: an agent that only tests what its answer predicts will not find a broader truth.

source: Klayman & Ha (1987) Confirmation, disconfirmation, and information in hypothesis testing
finding: Reframes Wason's 'confirmation bias' as a positive test strategy: test cases you expect to have the target property. Usually a good heuristic. It fails when the true rule is broader than the hypothesis (hypothesis nested inside the target set), where only negative tests (cases the hypothesis says should fail) can falsify.
numbers: Formal set model with false-positive and false-negative rates; positive tests find false positives only, negative tests find false negatives. When p(target) < .5 and p(target) = p(hypothesis), false positives exceed false negatives, so positive tests are often the more falsifying choice.
quote: many phenomena labeled confirmation bias are better understood in terms of a general positive test strategy
limits: Theory paper. Predictions depend on base rate of the target property and error types. Rule discovery with one-sided feedback is the worst case for positive testing.
agent_relevance: S4 should pick the test type from the structure: when the answer may be too narrow, test outside it; otherwise a positive test can falsify. 'Always try to refute' is not a universal rule.

source: Klayman & Ha (1987), review of earlier findings
finding: Positive testing was replicated across rule-discovery tasks (Mynatt et al. 1977, 1978; Mahoney 1976, 1979; Tweney et al. 1980; Wason and Johnson-Laird 1972; Klayman and Ha 1985). It eased when people had many test opportunities and no time pressure. Tweney et al. (1980) renamed feedback DAX (the rule) and MED (all else); people treated both as hypotheses, tested each positively, and solved far more often.
numbers: No sample sizes given in the review text for these studies.
limits: Secondary summary of the studies; the originals were not opened.
agent_relevance: Framing the complement as its own hypothesis (two-goal) makes negative tests natural; this became the Dual-Goal prompt used on LLMs in 2026.

source: Klayman & Ha (1987), extension to real tasks
finding: In social judgement people ask a supposed introvert 'Are you shy?' (yes if hypothesis true). Trope and Bassok (1983) found this only for extreme traits, matching the model: the rarer the target, the more positive tests help. Positive-only testing hurts because it never reveals false negatives.
numbers: Positive tests suit cases where false positives matter more or are more likely.
limits: Argument by analysis, not new data.
agent_relevance: Use positive tests for cheap breadth when false positives are the main risk; add negative tests when the answer may be too narrow.

source: Oaksford & Chater (1994) A rational analysis of the selection task as optimal data selection
finding: Bayesian model of choosing which card to turn by expected information gain. With a rarity assumption (p and q are rare) it predicts the usual choices and says the standard 'falsification' answer was judged against an outdated philosophy of science.
numbers: In the abstract selection task only 4% pick p and not-q; 46% pick p and q, 33% p alone, 7% p, q and not-q (Johnson-Laird and Wason 1970).
quote: performance on this task has been assessed against a now outmoded falsificationist philosophy of science
limits: Fit depends on the rarity assumption and a chosen prior; the model has been contested by later work not opened here.
agent_relevance: Test choice can be scored by expected information gain, not only 'can it refute'. A cheap rule for the schema: pick the test whose outcome most separates the live candidates.

source: Oaksford & Chater (1994), philosophical framing
finding: States that philosophers rejected strict falsificationism as unfaithful to the history of science (Kuhn, Lakatos) and unworkable (Duhem, Quine, Putnam, Churchland), and that Bayesian optimal data selection is the modern account of choosing experiments (Platt-style: test where hypotheses disagree).
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Their own position; strict Popperians disagree.
agent_relevance: Confirms the design choice: use falsification as a heuristic inside an information-seeking test choice, not as a dogma.

source: Abe et al. (2026) Deontic conditional reasoning in LLMs: Wason selection task
finding: LLMs do better on deontic (permission) rules than descriptive rules, as humans do. On the deontic rules their errors fit matching bias (picking cards named in the rule) better than confirmation bias.
numbers: Accuracy higher on deontic rules in all models and prompt types, by 5.0 to 41.2 percentage points; humans pick the correct p and not-q pair in under 10% of cases on the abstract task.
limits: Several open-weight models only (e.g. gemma-3-27b, qwen3-14b, olmo-2-32b); lexical matching may be confused with confirmation seeking.
agent_relevance: LLM test-choice errors may come from surface matching to the wording, so a falsifying test should be derived by code from the answer's structure, not left to wording.

source: Banatt, Cheng, Hwu (2024) WILT: Wason inductive logic test for LLMs
finding: First LLM version of 2-4-6: hidden Boolean function over three numbers, up to 30 tests, binary feedback. Best model solved 28% (14/50, Claude 3.5 Sonnet). Common failure: confirmation bias, with stronger models more likely to try to falsify.
numbers: Accuracy: Claude 3.5 Sonnet 14/50, o1-mini 13/50, o1-preview 12/50, chatgpt-4o-latest 11/50, Mistral Large 2 11/50, GPT-4o 9/50, Llama 3.1 405B 8/50, Claude 3 Haiku 1/50, Gemma 2 9B 0/50.
quote: a participant will identify a plausible hypothesis and continue to propose tests that attempt to confirm it
limits: N=50 tasks per model; 2024 models; mixing two or more models in a multi-turn run may beat one strong model.
agent_relevance: Baseline showing that multi-turn hypothesis testing is hard even for frontier models in 2024.

source: Jhaveri et al. (2026) Failing to Falsify: confirmation bias in language models
finding: 11 LLMs play a 2-4-6 style rule-discovery game (45 turns max, hidden rule consistent with 4 candidate rules). LLMs often test triples that fit their own guess. Task success ranges 6% to 78%. More disconfirming tests go with higher success.
numbers: Success 6% to 78%. Incompatible:compatible test ratio I:C; Spearman about 0.75 (thinking models) and 0.54 (non-thinking) between I:C and success (read from figure labels). Thinking vs non-thinking Qwen3-8B baseline success 0.21 vs 0.06. Dataset 4 rule sets x 4 rules, 80 test episodes.
quote: LLMs exhibit confirmation bias, often proposing triples to confirm their hypothesis rather than trying to falsify it
limits: Rules and judge are LLM-generated; correlation, not proof of cause; thinking-mode gains were not accompanied by a consistent rise in I:C.
agent_relevance: Measure our agent's share of tests that could contradict its current answer; this is a cheap code-side log.

source: Jhaveri et al. (2026) interventions: Dual-Goal and Think-in-Opposites
finding: Two human debiasing prompts help LLMs. Think-in-Opposites (pick a feature of the last test, test its opposite) raised task success in all models. Dual-Goal (guess the rule and its complement) helped in 8 of 11. Average rule discovery rose from 42% to 56%. Both raised I:C in 18 of 22 cases.
numbers: Qwen3-32B thinking: baseline 0.41, TiO 0.61; Qwen3-8B thinking 0.21 to 0.36; Llama-3.3-70B non-thinking 0.21 to 0.38; Qwen3-32B non-thinking Dual-Goal fell to 0.10.
limits: Significant for thinking models; for non-thinking models mixed (small gain with TiO, small drop with Dual-Goal). Table columns were hard to parse; some per-cell values may be misaligned.
agent_relevance: A forced 'test the opposite' step can help, but only gate it on a signal (G1): it hurt weak models.

source: Jhaveri et al. (2026) distillation and Blicket transfer
finding: Fine-tuning on Think-in-Opposites traces raised success (Qwen3-8B 0.21 to 0.35; Qwen3-32B 0.41 to 0.64) and transferred to a new task, the Blicket test. Transfer was smaller than prompting on the new task.
numbers: Cross-scale and intervention: 8B student from 32B teacher with TiO reached 0.59. Blicket: Qwen3-32B base 0.57, TiO prompt 0.86, Wason-distilled 32B 0.77; Qwen3-8B base 0.32, TiO 0.40, distilled about 0.34 to 0.38.
limits: Small models and one extra domain; Blicket hypotheses have no clean opposite.
agent_relevance: Falsification-style exploration can be learned and generalise a bit; our no-training scaffold should get it from the loop instead.

source: Bertolazzi, Tentori, Bernardi (2026) FalsifyBench
finding: Rule-discovery games built from WordNet categories (100 games, 12 LLMs). The hypothesis usually sits inside the target, as in 2-4-6, so only tests outside it can falsify. Reasoning models do far better. No model is near optimal.
numbers: Success: GPT-5.2-Chat 75%, GPT-OSS-120B 68%, best instruction-tuned DeepSeek-V3.1 41%, others 33 to 35%; small reasoning models worse (GPT-5-Nano 12%, Qwen3.5-9B 21%).
limits: Semantic categories not numbers; each LLM was both player and oracle, oracle errors measured (kappa 0.34 to 0.98).
agent_relevance: Strong evidence that negative testing is the driver; model size and reasoning mode matter first.

source: Bertolazzi et al. (2026) FalsifyBench: confirmation bias and falsification
finding: Share of positive tests ('confirmation bias') strongly predicts failure. Conclusive falsification rate is highest in reasoning models and falls with positive testing.
numbers: Spearman rho -0.779 (p=0.003) between confirmation bias and success; rho -0.937 (p<0.001) between confirmation bias and conclusive falsification rate. Positive-test share 24.2% to 39.0% for GPT-OSS-20B/GPT-5.2-Chat/GPT-5-Mini vs 66% to 82% for instruction-tuned. Conclusive falsification: GPT-OSS-20B 59.2%, GPT-OSS-120B 53.4%, GPT-5.2-Chat 49.5%, Llama-4-Maverick 18.0%, GPT-5-Nano 26.6%.
limits: 12 models, so correlations rest on 12 points; positive tests are bad here by design (hypothesis nested in target).
agent_relevance: Gives the metric for S4: share of tests that can conclusively falsify the current answer.

source: Bertolazzi et al. (2026) FalsifyBench: oracle quality and failure patterns
finding: Oracle skill does not explain success: MiniMax-M2.5, GLM-5 and GPT-5-Nano had similar oracle kappa but succeeded in 35%, 58% and 12% of games. A mixed-effects regression with oracle error rate as covariate still found player strategy mattered. Failed games had more positive tests.
numbers: Positive testing in failed vs successful games: GPT-5.2-Chat 50% vs 20%; GPT-OSS-20B 53% vs 17%. Not committing to a guess and exhausting the turn limit were other failure modes.
limits: Bayesian mixed-effects logistic fit; appendix details were skimmed only.
agent_relevance: Failure is partly a strategy problem the scaffold can fix, not only a knowledge problem.

source: Huang, Jin, Li, Li, Candes, Leskovec (2025) POPPER: agentic sequential falsification
finding: LLM agents turn a free-text hypothesis into measurable sub-hypotheses, run falsification experiments, convert each p-value to an e-value, and stop when the combined e-value passes 1/alpha. Gives Type-I error control with optional stopping. Six domains, 3 benchmarks.
numbers: Alpha 0.1, 5 runs. Baselines overshoot: Self-Refine Type-I 0.248 on DiscoveryBench, ReAct 0.145. POPPER stays near alpha (about 0.10 on DiscoveryBench). Higher power than controlled baselines (stated as 66.5% greater than ReAct on DiscoveryBench; 3.17x Self-Refine on TargetVal-IL2).
limits: The extracted Table 3 was garbled by PDF layout, so exact per-row POPPER numbers were not all verified; use headline claims only. Needs strong LLMs (Haiku 3.5 failed error control).
agent_relevance: Closest working design to S4 plus a stopping rule: accumulate evidence from independent tests; do not stop on one pass.

source: Huang et al. (2025) POPPER: human comparison and ablations
finding: Nine computational biologists did the same validation task. POPPER matched them in error and power but 9.7 times faster, with 3.6 times more code and 2.5 times more statistical tests. Removing the relevance checker inflated Type-I error because irrelevant nulls got 'falsified'.
numbers: N=9 experts; no significant difference at that sample size; POPPER-CodeGen Type-I 0.311 and 0.264 on DiscoveryBench and TargetVal-IL2.
limits: Small human sample; domain is gene-target validation; benchmark negatives built by the authors.
agent_relevance: A falsifying test must be relevant to the claim; an irrelevant test that 'fails' proves nothing. Add a relevance check (code or independent call).

source: Liu et al. (2024) AIGS / Baby-AIGS: falsification in AI-generated science
finding: Argues falsification is the core of research and adds a FalsificationAgent that picks significant results from an experiment log and runs ablations to check which factor is really responsible. Three tasks: data engineering, self-instruct alignment, language modelling.
numbers: Executability: Baby-AIGS almost 100% experiment and overall success vs AI Scientist 44.8% and 29.2% on selected tasks. Human experts scored its falsification process below top-conference papers (0 to 2 scales; importance score higher than consistency and correctness).
limits: Small human evaluation, authors' own tasks, preliminary. Agent proposes importance well but designs weak ablation plans.
agent_relevance: Ablation after a win is a falsification step: remove the claimed cause and see whether the win goes away. Worth an operator for result claims.

source: Batista & Griffiths (2026) A rational analysis of the effects of sycophantic AI
finding: A Bayesian agent fed examples sampled from its own hypothesis gets more sure but no closer to truth. Tested in a modified 2-4-6 task with a chatbot supplying sequences. Default GPT-5.1 behaved like explicit confirming feedback.
numbers: 557 Prolific participants (504 in discovery analysis). Discovery: random sequence 29.5%, rule disconfirming 14.1%, agreeable 11.8%, rule confirming 8.4%, default GPT 5.9%. Default vs random: 5.9% vs 29.5%, diff 23.6 pp. Confidence change: rule confirming +9.5, default +5.4, random -56.8. ANOVA F(4,507)=72.67, eta2=.36.
limits: Online sample, three rounds, even-number rule; Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite coded the final hypotheses; default vs rule-disconfirming only marginal.
agent_relevance: An answer supplied or checked by the model itself is sampled from its own beliefs, so a pass is weak (G4, G5). Evidence must come from outside, e.g. random draws.

source: Mossel (2026) LLMs, reasoning and plagiarism (Refutability gap)
finding: Argues claims that LLMs reason or discover do not meet Popper's refutability test because training data and transcripts are hidden. Lists pitfalls: is it really new, model updates, missing transcripts, missing failed attempts and counterfactuals.
numbers: No measurements; position paper.
limits: Opinion; its main claim is itself untested.
agent_relevance: Log every attempt and every failed test with the transcript, so that our own claims about the agent can be refuted.
